# Upāli Sutta (MN 56 (PTS MN i 371))
**ID:** MN 56 (PTS MN i 371)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)

**Title (Pali):** Upāli Sutta

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Upāli Sutta* (MN 56; PTS MN i 371) is the fifty-sixth discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [SuttaCentral]. The sutta recounts how the wealthy householder Upāli, an influential lay disciple and supporter of the Jains (Nigaṇṭhas), approaches the Buddha intending to debate and refute him on the doctrine of karma [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The discussion centers on the moral weight of actions: while the Jains viewed bodily action as the most severe form of "rod" or punishment (*daṇḍa*), the Buddha asserts that mental action (*mano-kamma*) and intention carry the greatest moral weight and blameworthiness [IABU 2012_a; Polak 2011; Martini; Peoples]. Engaging in dialectical, Socratic questioning, the Buddha demonstrates the internal contradictions of Upāli's position and converts him with what his critics described as his "converting magic" (*āvattanī māyā*) [Jayatilleke 1963; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Following Upāli's conversion, the Buddha delivers gradual instruction, and Upāli utters a celebrated concluding verse sequence containing a hundred epithets in praise of the Buddha, which reflects ancient motifs such as the "seven seers" (*isisattama*) [Shaw 2006; McTighe; Levman 2014].
Curated parallels include a full Chinese version in the *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 133), an Anguttara Nikāya parallel (AN 4.193), Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta 17; SF 72, 97, 109, 281, 286), and an entry in the Tibetan *Upāyikā* (Up 4.096) [SuttaCentral]. Upāli's concluding praise verses survive in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit under the title *Varṇaśatam*, as well as in Central Asian Turfan fragments that incorporate the thirty-two marks of the great man [Shaw 2006; Levman 2014; Dan Martin 2006]. Linguistic variations between the Pali verses (e.g., *pabhinnakhila*) and Central Asian Sanskrit equivalents (*prahīṇakhila*) provide philological evidence for intermediate translation stages, likely involving Gāndhārī [Levman 2014]. DharmaNexus identifies 3,520 Pali-internal reuse passages across 175 texts, showing particularly long formulaic overlaps with the *Mahākhandhaka* and *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* of the Vinaya, AN 8, and AN 4.193 [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language matching, DharmaNexus aligns the discourse closely with Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* fascicle 32 (ZH_T01_0026_032), fully corroborating the curated correspondence to MĀ 133 [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
